questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What a discussion rule redistributes
questions.learningObjective: Identify what a discussion rule redistributes among reviewers
questions.stem: A design review for a cast-aluminium bracket ends with a rule giving every engineer two minutes of uninterrupted floor time.

options.text: It redistributes conversational airtime, so quieter members can reach the record as often as senior ones.
It determines which design risks are discussed first, so a capped speaker can no longer hide a defect.
options.misconception: treats the rule as a priority scheme for technical risk

options.text: It settles the technical ranking of the bracket options, giving the chair a defensible order.
options.misconception: believes time limits decide which engineering risk matters

options.text: It replaces technical judgment entirely, since equal floor time makes all opinions equally credible.
options.misconception: assumes the rule ranks design risks rather than talk time

questions.explanation: A speaking-time rule governs who gets to say what and for how long, so it redistributes attention across participants. It does not rank technical risks, and equal airtime makes opportunity equal, not credibility equal.
questions.hint: Ask who gains floor time, not which risk is judged worst.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What a speaking-time rule produces
questions.learningObjective: Identify what a timed round of comments produces in a review record

stimulus.body: The design brief adds a rule that each reviewer gives a ninety-second summary of their objection before any discussion begins. The chair asks that summaries be read, not debated, during the round.

questions.stem: After the timed round has finished, what does it leave behind in the meeting record?

options.text: A settled agenda, because a timed summary leaves no ambiguity about which issue comes next.
options.misconception: believes a timed round settles the order of business on its own

options.text: A quality check on the objections, since the clock exposes claims that will not survive questioning.
options.misconception: thinks a clock can judge the strength of a technical objection

options.text: A queue of stated positions, which later discussion can attack without the round itself being attacked.
An equal contribution to the decision, since every reviewer now holds the floor for the same span.
options.misconception: assumes equal time produces equal influence on the outcome

questions.explanation: A timed round chiefly produces a recorded set of positions in a fixed order, so later discussion can engage them. Equal duration gives equal opportunity, not equal weight, and the clock says nothing about merit.
questions.hint: Think about what survives in writing after the round ends.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Argument against a rule against interruption
questions.learningObjective: Construct the argument against a rule against interruption
questions.stem: A colleague argues that your design brief should forbid interruption during design reviews, and asks you to assess the objection. Write the argument against the rule.

answer.exemplar: An argument against a rule against interruption holds that interruption often carries information the speaker did not plan to supply: a half-asked question can expose a hidden assumption before the conclusion is stated. The rule therefore does not merely remove noise; it removes the fastest route from a claim to its weakness, and it privileges whoever is most fluent when holding the floor uninterrupted.

questions.explanation: The task asks for the argument against the rule, not a summary of the rule. The strongest case says interruption is a diagnostic instrument: questions surface hidden assumptions early, which the rule removes.
questions.hint: Argue from what a question can reveal, not from politeness.

questions.learningObjective: Weigh the cost of a rule against personal remarks in reviews
questions.stem: A design review panel wants a rule banning personal remarks about colleagues, so members cannot be characterised. Which consideration most weakens the case for the rule?

options.text: Personal remarks are legally risky, which is why no professional panel should ever tolerate them.
options.misconception: assumes the objection is purely legal, not about argument

options.text: Rules of personal conduct belong in a code of ethics rather than in a design review meeting.
options.misconception: believes the issue is where the rule belongs, not its cost

options.text: Most engineers rarely make personal remarks, so the rule would protect no one from real harm.
options.misconception: assumes how often misconduct occurs settles the rule's value

options.text: The rule can push necessary criticism into tone, so substantive objections get re-labelled as personal and dropped.

questions.explanation: A rule against personal remarks can operate as a filter on criticism, since any objection can be presented as an attack on the person. The panel must weigh whether its review still surfaces the weaknesses in the design itself.
questions.hint: Ask which criticisms the rule would stop the group making.

questions.learningObjective: Trace how a ban on personal criticism reshapes a review

options.text: Criticism stops entirely, because no engineer can criticise a design without personal reference.
options.misconception: assumes the ban makes criticism impossible rather than blander

options.text: Discussion improves, because engineers now focus on drawings rather than on each other.
options.misconception: believes politeness automatically improves technical substance

options.text: The group splits into those who obey the rule and those who quietly stop attending reviews.
options.misconception: assumes withdrawal and non-compliance rather than cautious speech

options.text: Substantive criticism survives but becomes blander and safer, because critics now must attack only the design.

questions.explanation: A ban on personal attack reshapes criticism instead of removing it: critics still object but must phrase objections so no one reads them as personal. The cost is blunter argument under permanent caution.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: The standard set by intellectual honesty
questions.learningObjective: Apply the standard of intellectual honesty to a test report
questions.stem: In your design brief you must state how the load test came out. Which standard does intellectual honesty set here?

options.text: Report the result in the form most likely to keep the client's schedule, provided the margin is stated.
options.misconception: believes honesty allows framing truth to protect a schedule

options.text: Report the result as the test produced it, including the case where the failure margin was thin.
Report the result only once the design has been revised to pass comfortably, so no one worries.
options.misconception: assumes honesty means waiting until the numbers look good

options.text: Report the result as the worst plausible case, since caution about one's own data is the standard.
options.misconception: thinks honesty means pessimism rather than accurate reporting

questions.explanation: Intellectual honesty requires describing results as they came out, not as the designer would prefer them. Choosing a pessimistic spin is still a distortion, and framing the truth for schedule reasons is not reporting.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Risk of a norm of charitable interpretation
questions.learningObjective: Identify the risk created by a norm of charitable interpretation

stimulus.body: The design team has a norm that every objection is interpreted in the strongest possible sense before it is answered. In a recent review, an engineer's remark about the mast's fatigue life was read as a claim that the mast would fail in service.

questions.stem: Under this norm, what risk has the design team already accepted in its reviews?

options.text: An objection can be silently upgraded into a stronger claim, so the team answers a position nobody took.
Engineers will begin to soften their objections so that the norm does not inflate them.
options.misconception: assumes people speak more carefully rather than being misread

options.text: The meeting will spend its time on tone rather than on the fatigue calculation.
options.misconception: believes the risk is about meeting tone rather than misreading

options.text: Only the most senior engineers will be permitted to make brief remarks about the structure.
options.misconception: thinks charity norms mainly restrict who may speak briefly

questions.explanation: Charitable interpretation applied automatically can rewrite the speaker's claim into one they never made, and the group then answers that substitute. The failure is silent, because no one ever states the inflation aloud.
questions.hint: Check whether the team answered what was actually said.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Cost of a bare disagreement
questions.learningObjective: Explain the cost of a bare disagreement to a design team
questions.stem: A colleague ends a design review with 'I disagree' and nothing else. Explain what that bare disagreement costs the group.

answer.exemplar: A bare disagreement costs the group the information that would let it act on the objection. Without a reason, the team cannot tell whether the engineer disputes the analysis, the schedule, the code requirement, or simply the mood of the meeting, so the only available response is to ask again, which consumes more time than the disagreement would have.

questions.explanation: The item asks for a cost, and the cost is lost information, not lost politeness. A bare objection forces the group to spend time eliciting the reasoning that should have carried the objection.
questions.hint: Think about what the group cannot do next.

options.misconception: assumes restricting speakers improves technical scrutiny

options.text: The owner becomes the sole channel for information about the subsystem, including others' findings.
The group will detect design errors later, since the owner has time to prepare a complete defence.
options.misconception: believes preparation delay means later detection of errors

options.text: Review meetings shorten, because disagreements inside a subsystem are settled before they are raised.
options.misconception: thinks one-speaker rules remove the need to raise disagreements

questions.explanation: Naming one speaker concentrates the information channel as well as the floor, so other engineers' findings must pass through that owner. The design must judge whether the owner can be trusted to relay them.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What a rule against ad hominem costs
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a rule against ad hominem costs a team
questions.stem: Your design brief forbids ad hominem criticism of design proposals. Explain what this rule costs the team.

answer.exemplar: The cost is that the team loses its sharpest available tool for exposing a weak proposal, because a critique of the author's competence can cut through a polished argument faster than any technical objection. Without that route, engineers must find technical faults on the merits, which is slower and depends on everyone sharing the same engineering vocabulary.

questions.explanation: The task asks what the rule costs, so the answer must name a loss. The loss is a slower route to exposing a weak design, since personal criticism can no longer serve as a shortcut.
questions.hint: Name what the team can no longer do quickly.

options.misconception: believes dissent needs corroboration before it is recorded

options.text: The dissent is excluded whenever it could embarrass the client or delay the contract.
options.misconception: assumes honesty permits excluding costly dissent

options.text: The dissent is reproduced in full, whatever its evidential weight, since completeness is the only safeguard.
options.misconception: confuses verbatim recording with honest appraisal of the claim

options.text: The dissent is recorded as it was raised, without the writer softening it to protect consensus.

questions.explanation: The minutes record a discussion, so the honest course is to write the dissent as it was made. Filtering for tone distorts the record; ignoring evidential weight is a failure of judgment instead.
questions.hint: Decide whether minutes describe or adjudicate.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Argument against a rule against interruption
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a rule against interruption is worth contesting
questions.stem: Explain why a rule against interruption is worth contesting in a design review rather than accepted as good etiquette.

answer.exemplar: The rule is worth contesting because interruption is not merely noise; it is one of the fastest mechanisms a review has for testing a claim while the claim is still cheap to change. A question at the point of assertion can stop a designer building a later section on an untested assumption, and no summary at the end of the meeting recovers that moment.

questions.explanation: The task asks for a reason to contest the rule, so the answer must identify what the rule removes: the early, cheap chance to test a claim while the design can still absorb a correction.
questions.hint: Argue about timing, not about manners.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: The standard set by intellectual honesty
questions.learningObjective: Respond to an objection to a charitable reading rule

stimulus.body: A chair circulates guidance that all objections in design reviews will be understood in the most favourable sense the speaker could have intended. A senior engineer objects that the rule would let a weak proposal be defended by inflating any mild criticism into a serious one.

questions.stem: How should the chair respond to the senior engineer's objection?

options.text: By insisting the rule is standard practice, since few reviewers have ever challenged it before.
options.misconception: appeals to practice instead of to the objection's substance

options.text: By dropping the rule entirely, since any guidance that can be challenged should never be adopted.
options.misconception: reacts to the possibility of challenge, not to the risk

options.text: By keeping the rule and warning the engineer that objections of this kind will be noted against them.
options.misconception: disciplines the objector instead of fixing the rule

options.text: By conceding the risk and requiring the speaker to confirm the strengthened reading before answering.

questions.explanation: The objection identifies a real defect, and the cheapest repair is a confirmation step: the speaker must accept the strengthened reading before the team answers. Dropping the rule overrules a concern; warnings avoid it.
questions.hint: Look for a repair that keeps the rule usable.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Risk of a norm of charitable interpretation
questions.learningObjective: Explain what honesty requires of a successful team
questions.stem: Explain what a standard of intellectual honesty requires of a design team that has had good results.

answer.exemplar: Good results do not relax the standard; they test it. A team that has been right often enough may come to trust its instincts, and that trust is exactly where honest reporting begins to fail, because the confident prediction gets reported as though it were a measured result. Intellectual honesty requires that the team keep describing predictions as predictions and results as results, however good its recent record.

questions.explanation: The task asks what the standard requires given good results, so the answer must reject the idea that success relaxes the obligation. The requirement is to keep predictions and results clearly distinguished however confident the team has become.
questions.hint: Do not let the track record do the reasoning.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Cost of a bare disagreement
questions.learningObjective: Identify the change that reduces the cost of bare disagreement
questions.stem: Which change would most reduce the cost of a bare disagreement in a design review?

options.text: Require the objector to state the specific decision or assumption the objection concerns.
Allow the chair to award extra speaking time to whichever member spoke most recently.
options.misconception: rewards the last speaker rather than the informative one

options.text: Publish the number of objections raised by each member at the end of the review.
options.misconception: adds a reputational cost to raising objections

options.text: Require all disagreements to be settled privately with the chair before the meeting begins.
options.misconception: removes disagreement from the group rather than making it useful

questions.explanation: A bare objection lacks a reason; naming the decision or assumption at issue supplies that reason and makes it actionable. The alternatives reward volume, penalise objectors, or hide disagreement.
questions.hint: Fix the missing part, not the speaker.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What a discussion rule redistributes
questions.learningObjective: Determine what a discretionary speaking-time rule produces
questions.stem: A design brief lets the chair allocate speaking time as the chair sees fit. What does this rule produce, and what does it risk?

options.text: An equal distribution of attention, since the chair is expected to use the discretion fairly.
options.misconception: assumes discretion produces equality rather than variability

options.text: A shorter meeting, since the chair allocates only the time the agenda actually requires.
options.misconception: believes a chair's discretion shortens meetings

options.text: A neutral record, since the chair's allocation is written down and can be checked later.
options.misconception: confuses recording the allocation with neutralising it

options.text: Discretion over the floor, so the distribution of attention depends on the chair's judgement.

questions.explanation: The rule hands the chair discretion over who speaks and for how long, so the distribution of attention rests on the chair's judgement rather than a stated rule. Recording the allocation does not change its effect.
questions.hint: Follow who actually decides the floor.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What a speaking-time rule produces
questions.learningObjective: Identify what a single-turn speaking rule produces
questions.stem: A speaking-time rule lets each participant take one uninterrupted turn of any length. What does the rule produce?

options.text: An equal contribution, since one turn each gives everyone the same opportunity.
options.misconception: assumes one turn each equals equal airtime

options.text: A predictable agenda, since each turn has a known length that can be timed in advance.
options.misconception: believes turns have a known fixed length

options.text: A turn-taking structure in which length is set by the speaker's own estimate of importance.
A condensed meeting, since speakers usually aim for brevity when they know they cannot be interrupted.
options.misconception: infers brevity from the absence of interruption

questions.explanation: One turn each produces turn-taking, with length set by each speaker's own sense of what matters. Equal opportunity is not equal airtime, no length is fixed, and being left uninterrupted does not shorten speech.
questions.hint: Ask what determines the length of a turn.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Argument against a rule against interruption
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a review outcome under a no-interruption rule

stimulus.body: During a load-path review, a designer says the bracket will carry the full shear. A colleague begins 'but did you check...' and is cut off by the chair under the no-interruption rule. The design is approved that afternoon.

questions.stem: What does this sequence show about the effect of the rule on the design review?

options.text: A confirmation that the rule works, since the meeting finished on time with a decision recorded.
options.misconception: treats a recorded decision as evidence of checking

options.text: The question that might have exposed a weak assumption was removed, so the record shows untested agreement.
A scheduling gain, since the design was approved in a single afternoon without an extra session.
options.misconception: counts a fast approval as evidence the rule helped

options.text: A tone improvement, since no member had to be asked to stop speaking over another.
options.misconception: reads the outcome as evidence about the meeting's atmosphere

questions.explanation: The rule removed the one question that addressed the unchecked assumption, so the approval rests on a claim nobody tested. A decision recorded the same afternoon shows the meeting ran, not that the load path was verified.
questions.hint: Separate the fact of approval from the fact of checking.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Cost of a bare disagreement
questions.learningObjective: Identify what a bare disagreement costs a review group

stimulus.body: At a fatigue-life review of a welded mast, an engineer says only 'I disagree with this' and adds nothing further. The chair moves to the next agenda item, and the minutes record the objection with no reason attached.

questions.stem: What does this bare disagreement cost the design team?

options.text: Which decision the objection targets, so the group can neither test the claim nor revise the design.
Review time, because the chair must pause the review to elicit a reason from the engineer.
options.misconception: counts elapsed time instead of the missing information

options.text: The engineer's credibility, since an unexplained objection weakens that member's standing later.
options.misconception: locates the cost in the speaker's reputation

options.text: The chair's authority, since a member refuses to justify an objection in public.
options.misconception: identifies a status cost rather than an informational one

questions.explanation: A bare objection names no reason, so the group cannot tell whether it targets the weld, the load case, or the code, and can neither test the claim nor record it usefully.
questions.hint: Ask what the group still cannot do with the objection.
